# Plan a Week of Family Dinners With One AI Prompt

> **In short:** Tell a free AI assistant your family's tastes, your budget, and the nights you're slammed, and it will hand you back a 7-day dinner plan plus one grocery list. The same prompt works in ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or Copilot.

You don't need a recipe app, a spreadsheet, or a stack of cookbooks to plan a week of dinners. You need one paragraph about your family, typed into an AI assistant (an AI is a tool you can have a conversation with by typing or speaking). Twenty minutes later you'll have dinners for seven nights and a shopping list you can photograph at the store. Here's how to do it without any prior experience.

## Before you start
- An account on a free AI assistant — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or Copilot all work, and the steps below look the same in each.
- A phone, tablet, or computer with internet access.
- A rough idea of this week's food budget (a number, not a plan) and which nights are busiest.
- About 15 minutes the first time, five minutes once you get the hang of it.
- The free plan is enough. Paid tiers let the assistant remember longer conversations, which is nice, but not required here.

## Step 1 — Open a new chat and start with one sentence
Open your AI assistant's website or app and tap the button that starts a new conversation. You'll see a blank box — that empty space is called the prompt field, and what you type there is called a prompt (just a fancy word for "your instruction to the AI"). The box is usually at the bottom of the screen with a send arrow on the right.
💬 Example: `I need help planning a week of family dinners.`
You'll know it worked when the assistant replies (usually within a few seconds) with something like "Sure, I'd be happy to help" and maybe a follow-up question.

## Step 2 — Tell the AI who it's cooking for
Before the assistant can plan meals, it needs to know the people. In plain words, describe your family: how many eaters, any picky members, allergies or foods you avoid (pork, shellfish, nuts, dairy), and a general taste — comfort food, light and fresh, kid-friendly, adventurous. Look for the same prompt box from Step 1; just keep typing or hit Enter to start a new line. If you're on a phone and the keyboard is in the way, tap the text field again to bring it back.
💬 Example: `Family of 4: two adults and two kids (ages 6 and 9). One adult is lactose intolerant. We like simple comfort food — pasta, rice bowls, sheet-pan dinners. No shellfish or very spicy food.`
You'll know it worked when the assistant summarizes your family back to you, which means it actually read what you wrote. If it just dives into recipes, gently repeat the family details before moving on.

## Step 3 — Add the practical limits
This is the step most people skip, and it's the one that makes the difference between a fun plan and a realistic one. Tell the assistant: your weekly budget (a rough number is fine), the nights you're too tired to cook (and need a 20-minute meal or a leftover night), any equipment you don't have (no oven, no blender, no air fryer), and whether anyone eats the same thing for lunch the next day (leftovers welcome). Type this in the same prompt box. The assistant keeps everything you wrote in the conversation, so just add a new line.
💬 Example: `Budget: about $120 for the week. Tuesdays and Thursdays are slammed (ballet + late meetings) so those nights need to be 20 minutes max, no fancy steps. We have a full kitchen (oven, stovetop, slow cooker) but no air fryer. Leftovers are great for lunch.`
You'll know it worked when the assistant acknowledges at least two of those limits back to you, like "Got it — quick Tuesday meals and a $120 budget." If it ignores them, ask it to "re-read my constraints and confirm" before continuing.

## Step 4 — Ask for the 7-day plan
Now for the actual ask. Type a single clear request: a 7-day dinner plan that respects everything you've said, with each day showing the meal name and a one-line description. Keep the request small and specific — the more you ask for in one message, the more the assistant has to guess about. If your assistant has a "tone" or "style" setting somewhere, you can ignore it; the default is fine. Look for the same prompt box, type your request, and hit send.
💬 Example: `Based on all of that, please give me a 7-day dinner plan (Monday through Sunday). For each day, show the meal name and one short line about what it is. Keep Tuesday and Thursday under 20 minutes. Aim for variety — no pasta two nights in a row.`
You'll know it worked when you see seven labeled days, each with a meal and a short description. If the plan looks like a generic list (the same chicken recipe every night), tell it: "More variety please — different proteins and cuisines across the week" and ask it to try again.

## Step 5 — Ask follow-up questions about any meal you don't recognize
Before you commit to the plan, scan it. If any meal name is unfamiliar ("what on earth is a shakshuka?"), ask the assistant right there in the same chat. Don't open a new conversation — the assistant already knows your family and budget, and will give a better answer with that context. A good prompt for this is "Explain [meal] in two sentences and tell me if kids usually like it." If your screen looks different after a long reply, scroll up — the assistant's answer will be just above the prompt box where you can keep typing.
💬 Example: `Quick check — what's "sheet-pan honey garlic chicken" in plain terms, and would my 6-year-old likely eat it?`
You'll know it worked when you get a short, plain-language description and a yes/no/maybe answer about the kids. If the assistant writes a 500-word essay, follow up with "Shorter please — two sentences" and it will tighten up.

## Step 6 — Build the grocery list in the same chat
Once the plan feels right, ask for the matching shopping list. The key is to ask for it in a specific shape: organized by store section (produce, dairy, pantry, meat, frozen), with quantities, and only listing ingredients that show up in the plan. This is where the AI really saves you time — it would take a human an hour to cross-reference seven recipes. Type in the same prompt box, same conversation.
💬 Example: `Great, the plan works. Now please build me one grocery list for the whole week, grouped by store section (produce, dairy, meat, pantry, frozen, other). List each item with the quantity I need. Only include things used in the plan.`
You'll know it worked when you see clear section headers and a quantity next to each item. If it dumps one long unsorted list, just say "Please regroup that by store section" and try again — this is the easiest fix and the assistant handles it instantly.

## Step 7 — Save it somewhere you'll actually find on Monday
The list is useless if it's buried in a chat you'll never reopen. Take a screenshot of the meal plan and the grocery list, or copy-paste them into your phone's notes app. If your AI assistant has a "share" or "bookmark" icon (often a bookmark ribbon or a little upward arrow at the top of the conversation), tap that to save the whole chat. Some assistants also let you email the conversation to yourself — look for a paper-airplane or share button. Pick whichever feels easiest; the goal is having the list in your pocket at the store.
💬 Example: Screenshot the grocery list grouped by section, then text it to yourself so it shows up in your messages.
You'll know it worked when you can open the list on your phone in the grocery aisle without searching through old chats. If you can't find the list by Sunday evening, take two minutes now to forward it to yourself — five minutes of friction here saves you forty minutes of "what did I plan?" on Monday morning.

## Common mistakes
- **Vague budget or none at all.** "We're on a budget" means nothing to an AI — it has no idea if that's $50 or $500. Always give a number. Fix: pick the roughest number ("about $100 a week") and the assistant will scale to it.
- **Asking for the grocery list in a new chat.** If you start fresh, the assistant forgets the plan and may invent ingredients. Fix: always stay in the same conversation from Step 1 through Step 6.
- **Forgetting the "no fancy equipment" limit.** The assistant loves suggesting air fryers, Instant Pots, and immersion blenders because those recipes look good. Fix: list your real equipment in Step 3, even if it feels obvious.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the dreaded Sunday "what are we eating?" question takes 10 minutes instead of 90, and your week starts calmer because the first grocery run is already mapped.
- **For your business or work:** the same prompt structure (describe the situation, set the limits, ask for a plan, then a checklist) works for client meeting prep, travel itineraries, and weekly project planning — the meal plan is just the most fun place to learn it.
- **If you're just getting started:** AI assistants are good at exactly this kind of "lots of small decisions bundled together" task. Once you trust them with dinner, try them with packing lists, party planning, or your weekly schedule.

## Try it now
Open your AI assistant right now and type the prompt from Step 4 — but use your own family details, not the examples. By the time your coffee is ready, you'll have a 7-day plan on your screen and a grocery list one message away.
